title: Character Avatars / NPCs
author: EfficientDivide1572
selftext:
Hey everyone! I'm making my own game with AI assisted tools + Claude Code. I set up my pipeline so with the editor I do a pretty fair portion of the work, only when engine changes need to be made then Claude goes into it.

I have reached a pretty serious bottleneck though. While I'm fine at designing homes/interiors/landscapes with the tools given, the character avatars have been EXTREMELY difficult to work with.

Postures are weird / movements uncanny / armour is hard to fit.

  
I rented a GPU and set up a comfy workflow and to that it seems like it has reached a bottleneck. the 3d models come out awkward and nothing is coming up to standard. I want semi-realistic fortnite(ish) character design. I tried some free assets too (Fantasy pack but because my game is an MMO they look awkward from afar / movement.

I've also tried importing my own character rigs/movements that I filmed myself doing but it's not mapping correctly.

Is Tripo/Meshy the only answer to this?

I really want to keep things as local as possible when it comes to asset creation, but are using the above tools the only way? Or are there other pretty solid routes to go before giving up on my local asset creation?

  
1) I need base character creation character  
2) NPC types - | Old | Rough | Blacksmiths | Artist   
3) Humanoid types - | Goblins | Warewolves | etc etc.

What would be the best way forward?  
Also sorry if this has been asked before, I just couldn't find anything specifically for MMORPGs

comments.author: weodawg
comments.body:
I recommend buying one player character asset that fits your style or is close enough. Use blender mcp to tweak it as you see fit. You want a high quality player character. 

For NPCs I’m doing meshy plus blender

comments.author: Mindestiny
comments.body:
If you want *honesty*?  You're not going to copy fortnite with a rented GPU running a comfy workflow.  Even the best models are still very janky and not production quality, and open source free mocap and rigging is... honestly terrible quality that requires a lot of professional touch up.  There's simply no way you're going to generate Fortnite-art-team quality with existing tooling as a solo dev. Maybe if you were Pixar and you had a team of engineers working on a fully in-house custom genAI solution.  But I'm gonna guess you're not.

The only way to truly get what you want at this time is hire a professional who knows how to do this the non-AI way.

replies.author: ai_dad_says_hi
replies.body: If you’re willing to pay for all the tech setup to generate the character assets, why not try paying a person? Of course there’s risk you pay for something you ultimately don’t like, but might be worth a shot. Also, iteration with an artist might help refine your ideas anyways.

replies.author: EfficientDivide1572
replies.body: So here's what I ended up doing - Tripo smart mesh, then had my cousin who's a 3d artist clean it up in blender. It came out really good, he used a bunch of tools, then he followed my direction for both characters. So pumped! My cousin rigged it, and got the motion all good too.

comments.author: Opening_Wafer_6584
comments.body:
Hey, Alex here from the Tripo Studio US team. The character side is definitely a different problem than environments, especially once you add armor, animation, and MMO-scale variation.

For the kind of semi-realistic stylized characters you’re describing, I’d probably think of Tripo more as a way to get a strong base mesh / character starting point rather than expecting one generation to solve the entire avatar pipeline.

The part I’m most curious about is where things are breaking down for you right now. Is the bigger issue getting a clean base character, fitting armor consistently, or getting the rig / animation to behave correctly afterward?

If you’re trying to support a lot of NPC archetypes, that distinction probably matters quite a bit for what workflow makes the most sense.
